title: Acme Bank Security Review — SIEM-ready Audit Export (beta)
summary: Acme Bank security/compliance review focused on Redwood’s SIEM-ready audit export beta for Splunk (HEC). Redwood walked through audit event schema v2 (event_id, timestamps, actor, action, resource, workspace/tenant), delivery semantics (at-least-once with retries + checkpointing; customer dedup via event_id), retention vs export responsibilities, backfill limits during beta, RBAC for export configuration, encryption/secret handling (TLS, KMS, SSE-KMS for S3; encrypted token storage for Splunk). Acme asked for evidence language for SOC2/ISO questionnaires, details on what fields are included/excluded for PII, and operational visibility (lag, last success, last error) and alerting options. Call ended with action items: Redwood to send Security FAQ, sample events, and draft IAM/HEC configuration guidance; Acme to confirm Splunk HEC endpoints/allowlist and desired index/sourcetype conventions.
topics: Audit event schema v2 (event_id, categories, actor/resource fields)
PII minimization/redaction (IP/user agent rules, prohibited payloads)
Delivery semantics: at-least-once, retries/backoff, dedup expectations
Checkpointing, replay/backfill behavior and beta limitations
RBAC and least-privilege permissions for export management
Encryption in transit/at rest; secret handling; KMS considerations
Operational visibility: exporter lag/health, status endpoints, dashboards
Beta scope: hosted + dedicated only; Private/on-prem follow-on
questions: Do audit events include source IP and user agent for all actions, and can those be suppressed for privacy?
Is delivery exactly-once or at-least-once, and how should Splunk deduplicate?
What is Redwood’s retention period for audit logs vs customer retention in Splunk?
What is the max backfill window in beta, and what happens during downstream outages (429/503)?
Who can create/modify export destinations, rotate tokens, and view delivery status?
Are Splunk HEC tokens stored encrypted and are they ever logged or exposed to support?
action_items: Redwood (Kevin Osei) to send Security FAQ language covering retention vs export responsibilities, at-least-once semantics, and beta scope disclaimers by 2025-03-10.
Redwood (Colin O'Donnell) to share Splunk HEC internal integration guide snippet: recommended index/source/sourcetype + HEC batching expectations by 2025-03-10.
Redwood (Simran Kaur) to provide 5–10 sample audit events (JSON) demonstrating event_id, category, actor/resource fields, and redaction patterns by 2025-03-11.
Acme (Tom Alvarez) to confirm Splunk HEC endpoint (hostname), required TLS inspection/proxy constraints, and outbound allowlist needs by 2025-03-12.
Acme (Mark Denson) to confirm desired Splunk parsing conventions (CIM mapping preference, sourcetype naming) and alerting expectations for export lag by 2025-03-12.
Redwood (Liam O'Rourke) to schedule a 30-min technical follow-up to walk through HEC test event validation and success criteria for beta onboarding by 2025-03-13.
next_steps: Redwood to send security FAQ + sample events + Splunk HEC setup notes.
Acme to confirm Splunk HEC details and any egress allowlisting requirements.
Set up a short follow-up to validate a test export into Acme’s Splunk dev index and confirm dedup/search queries.
If aligned, proceed with beta enablement request and RBAC verification for Acme tenant admins.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-03-06
Time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Title: Acme Bank Security Review — SIEM-ready Audit Export (beta)
Attendees (Redwood): Liam O'Rourke, Simran Kaur, Colin O'Donnell, Kevin Osei
Attendees (Acme Bank): Priya Shah, Mark Denson, Elaine Wu, Tom Alvarez

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
Summary: (see summary field)
Topics: audit schema, SIEM export, retention/backfill, RBAC, encryption

Transcript
[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, I think we’re at time. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Liam, I’m the TAM on the Acme account. The goal today is security and compliance review specifically for the SIEM-ready audit export beta. Priya, Mark, Elaine, Tom — thanks for making time.
[00:15] Priya Shah: Yep, thanks Liam. We’re mainly trying to close out the open questions from our vendor intake. We saw the beta note and we want to understand what’s real today versus roadmap.
[00:25] Liam O'Rourke: Totally. And just setting expectation up front: beta is hosted and dedicated deployments first. Private / on-prem patterns we can discuss at a high level but we’re not committing to support that in beta.
[00:37] Elaine Wu: That’s fine. We are currently hosted with you, but we do have regulated workloads that might go dedicated, so I’ll want to understand that boundary.
[00:45] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Quick intros on Redwood side: Simran is solutions architect, Colin is our solutions engineer who’s been deep in the Splunk integration, and Kevin is security engineering — audit semantics and policy.
[00:57] Kevin Osei: Hey all.
[01:00] Colin O'Donnell: Hi everyone.
[01:02] Simran Kaur: Hey.

[01:07] Liam O'Rourke: Priya, do you want to kick off with top questions?
[01:11] Priya Shah: Sure. Biggest ones: 1) what audit events are actually included, 2) do you have delivery guarantees for SIEM export, 3) retention and backfill — like if Splunk is down for a day, what happens, and 4) RBAC — who can configure exports and who can see delivery status.
[01:29] Mark Denson: And from SOC: we need to know if this is at-least-once and how we dedupe. Also what the “event id” looks like, because Splunk dedupe is always… fun.
[01:41] Tom Alvarez: I’m also looking for network patterns. Is this outbound from your side to our HEC endpoint, and do you support allowlists, and TLS validation, that kind of stuff.

[01:53] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. Kevin, can you start with audit event schema and what’s in/out from a privacy lens?
[02:00] Kevin Osei: Yep. So we have what we call audit event schema v2. The key differences: every event has a stable event_id, timestamp fields, a category taxonomy, and consistent actor/action/resource. The intent is that it maps cleanly into SIEMs.
[02:16] Kevin Osei: Required fields — generally: event_id, emitted_at (timestamp), observed_at depending on the producer, tenant_id/workspace_id, actor.type (user, service account, api key), actor.id, action, resource.type, resource.id, and outcome (success/failure) plus a reason code if there’s a failure.
[02:37] Elaine Wu: When you say actor.id, is that like email address?
[02:40] Kevin Osei: Good question. For human users, it’s a stable internal user identifier. We avoid raw email in the canonical fields. We may include a display string in some cases but it’s subject to our PII minimization rules. The idea is: you can correlate with your IdP via your own mapping, but the audit event itself shouldn’t leak more than necessary.
[03:02] Priya Shah: Does it include IP and user agent? That can be sensitive but we also need it.
[03:07] Kevin Osei: It’s “where applicable.” For interactive console actions and certain API calls, we capture source_ip and user_agent. For internal service-to-service actions, it’s often absent. Also, there’s policy that we do not log full request payloads, prompts, or model outputs in audit events.
[03:27] Mark Denson: Ok, so no prompts, no completions. That’s good.
[03:31] Kevin Osei: Right. We’ll log the fact that an API key created a model deployment change, or changed an export config, but not the content of what you ran.

[03:43] Colin O'Donnell: Just to add, in the SIEM export, we send those same audit events. We don’t create a separate “SIEM event” with extra fields, because that can drift.
[03:51] Tom Alvarez: So the export is basically a stream of the audit log.
[03:54] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[03:58] Priya Shah: Categories — can you give examples?
[04:02] Kevin Osei: Sure. Examples: auth.*, access.*, org.*, billing.*, model.*, deployment.*, key_management.*, audit_export.*. The exact list we’ll send as part of the beta pack.
[04:16] Priya Shah: We’ll need that list.
[04:18] Kevin Osei: Yep, we can provide it. And you can filter on categories and actions.

[04:24] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk delivery semantics — Mark’s question on dedupe. Colin?
[04:30] Colin O'Donnell: So the exporter is at-least-once delivery. Meaning: we may deliver the same event more than once under retry conditions, but we aim to never drop events within the retention/backfill window. The primary key for dedup is event_id.
[04:48] Mark Denson: So not exactly-once.
[04:50] Colin O'Donnell: Correct, not exactly-once. Exactly-once across Splunk HEC, network failures, retries — it’s not realistic. Instead we do: checkpointing + retries with backoff. And we strongly recommend dedup in Splunk by event_id.
[05:08] Mark Denson: What’s the format of event_id? UUID?
[05:11] Colin O'Donnell: It’s UUID-ish, yeah. It’s globally unique. We can share examples.
[05:15] Kevin Osei: It’s stable per event and deterministic from the event emission path, not like “random per export.” So retries keep the same event_id.

[05:26] Priya Shah: What about ordering? Like if someone disables an API key and then tries to use it, order matters.
[05:33] Colin O'Donnell: We don’t guarantee strict global ordering across all categories. In practice, within a tenant and within a short window, it’s close, but because we’re batching and exporting asynchronously, you should treat it as near-real-time with some reordering possible. Timestamps are authoritative.
[05:52] Priya Shah: Okay.

[05:55] Tom Alvarez: On HEC, Splunk can 429 you. How do you handle that?
[05:59] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. We handle 429 with exponential backoff and a circuit breaker per destination token. We also cap batch sizes and compress payloads. If Splunk is throttling, export lag increases; we surface that in status.
[06:18] Mark Denson: And does it drop after some time?
[06:20] Colin O'Donnell: It shouldn’t drop inside the backfill window. If it exceeds max lag, we can auto-pause the export to protect the system, and you can resume after issues are cleared.
[06:32] Priya Shah: Auto-pause sounds… scary. That means we stop getting events.
[06:37] Colin O'Donnell: It’s a safety mechanism. The idea is: if downstream is down for long enough, we don’t want unbounded queue growth or repeated hammering. When paused, we keep checkpoint state and you can resume, and we’ll replay from last checkpoint.

[06:57] Elaine Wu: Let’s define “backfill window.” What’s the actual number?
[07:01] Liam O'Rourke: In beta, the default backfill that you can request on config is up to 7 days. Kevin, correct me if that’s changed.
[07:08] Kevin Osei: That’s right for beta. There’s also Redwood internal retention of the underlying audit stream, which is longer than 7 days, but the “customer-configurable backfill” is 7 days in beta.
[07:20] Elaine Wu: What’s your retention for audit logs?
[07:24] Kevin Osei: For hosted, we retain audit events for 90 days in our control plane logging system today. Export is considered the customer’s long-term retention mechanism.
[07:35] Elaine Wu: Can you put that in writing for SOC2 questionnaires?
[07:38] Kevin Osei: Yes, we have standard evidence language: Redwood retains audit logs for a defined period and customers are responsible for downstream retention once exported. We’ll send you the language.

[07:52] Priya Shah: So scenario: Splunk is down for 36 hours. We come back. Do we lose anything?
[07:59] Colin O'Donnell: If Splunk is down, exporter retries. Lag grows. If it crosses max lag threshold, it pauses. When you resume, we replay from checkpoint, subject to the backfill window and retention. If it’s within 7 days, you should be able to recover.
[08:18] Priya Shah: And if it’s 10 days?
[08:20] Colin O'Donnell: In beta, that’s where we’re limited. We’d need to handle it case-by-case. GA roadmap includes longer backfill and tooling.
[08:30] Elaine Wu: Ok, so we need that clearly stated as a limitation.
[08:33] Liam O'Rourke: Agreed.

[08:36] Mark Denson: For dedupe in Splunk: do you recommend using event_id as _key or in a lookup?
[08:43] Colin O'Donnell: Typically you ingest event_id as a field. Then you can use Splunk’s dedup command or a summary index approach. We can share recommended SPL. Most customers do dedup in correlation searches rather than at index-time, because index-time dedup can be tricky.
[08:59] Mark Denson: Right.

[09:02] Tom Alvarez: Network: does Redwood call our Splunk? Or do we pull?
[09:06] Colin O'Donnell: For Splunk HEC, it’s outbound push from Redwood to your HEC endpoint. You provide the endpoint URL and token. We validate destination hostnames against an allowlist pattern on our side to reduce SSRF and misconfig.
[09:22] Tom Alvarez: Can you support IP allowlisting from your egress?
[09:26] Colin O'Donnell: We can provide our egress IP ranges by region for hosted. For dedicated, it depends on how your dedicated cluster is configured, but yes we can support stable egress addresses.
[09:39] Tom Alvarez: We’ll need those ranges.
[09:41] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll include that in the follow-up.

[09:46] Priya Shah: Encryption: TLS, token storage, at rest.
[09:50] Kevin Osei: In transit: TLS 1.2+ for all destinations. For Splunk HEC specifically, we require HTTPS; we validate certs — no plain HTTP.
[10:02] Kevin Osei: At rest: the exporter uses encrypted storage for checkpoints and queues. Secrets like HEC tokens are stored encrypted using our KMS-backed secrets store. Access is restricted to the exporter service identity.
[10:18] Priya Shah: Are tokens ever logged?
[10:20] Kevin Osei: No. We treat them as secrets. They are redacted from logs and not included in audit events. Also, support staff do not have direct access to raw tokens.
[10:31] Elaine Wu: “Not have direct access” — do you have break glass?
[10:35] Kevin Osei: There is controlled break-glass for production incidents, with approvals and audit trails, but it is not used to view customer secrets. The access path is designed to avoid exposing secrets; operational actions are things like rotating references, disabling an export, etc.

[10:54] Mark Denson: Do you log admin actions like “export config changed”?
[10:58] Kevin Osei: Yes. Changes to export configuration are themselves audit events under audit_export.* category, including who changed it and what was changed at a high level (not the secret value).
[11:13] Priya Shah: That’s good.

[11:16] Liam O'Rourke: On RBAC, I’ll let Kevin and Colin tag-team. Who can configure exports.
[11:22] Kevin Osei: The model is least privilege. There are specific permissions: view audit exports, manage audit exports, rotate credentials reference, and view delivery status.
[11:34] Kevin Osei: Default roles: Org Admin typically can manage exports; Security Auditor role can view configuration and status but not modify destinations. You can customize roles if you have custom RBAC.
[11:49] Elaine Wu: Can you separate “view events” vs “view status”? Sometimes GRC wants evidence of controls but not necessarily operational details.
[11:56] Kevin Osei: Yes. “View delivery status” is separate from “view audit logs.” And the export feature is also gated behind a feature flag per tenant during beta.

[12:09] Priya Shah: And does the act of exporting create additional data exposure? Like can a rogue admin point it to their own Splunk?
[12:16] Kevin Osei: That’s a core threat model point. Mitigations include: RBAC boundaries, destination validation, and we recommend customers restrict who has manage privileges. Also, we can restrict allowed destination domains per tenant in some cases. In beta, it’s more manual, but it’s on the roadmap.
[12:34] Tom Alvarez: Is there an egress allowlist enforcement?
[12:37] Colin O'Donnell: We have hooks to validate destinations. For Splunk, we validate hostname and scheme. For S3, we validate bucket ownership patterns if using cross-account role. For Datadog it’s fixed endpoints.

[12:54] Priya Shah: Wait, so you support Datadog too?
[12:57] Liam O'Rourke: In beta, initial destinations are Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs intake, and generic S3 delivery. For Acme, we understand you’re Splunk-first.
[13:07] Mark Denson: Yes, Splunk.

[13:10] Elaine Wu: On data residency: we operate US only for this pilot. Any cross-region movement?
[13:16] Kevin Osei: Export runs within the region your Redwood control plane and tenant are in. We don’t intentionally ship audit events across regions for export. If you choose a Splunk endpoint in a different geography, then that’s your routing choice.
[13:31] Tom Alvarez: That’s fine.

[13:34] Mark Denson: Operational visibility: how do we know if exports are failing? Are there alerts? Or is it just a dashboard.
[13:41] Colin O'Donnell: There’s a status endpoint that the Redwood Console surfaces: export lag, last successful delivery timestamp, and last error message (sanitized). Internally we have dashboards and alerts. For customers, during beta we can set up notifications via support, but customer-configurable alert webhooks is likely GA.
[14:02] Mark Denson: So we can’t get an immediate alert today.
[14:05] Liam O'Rourke: Not self-serve in beta. What we can do is agree on an SLO and we’ll proactively monitor. Also we can provide guidance on querying “last seen event” in Splunk.
[14:18] Priya Shah: We’ll probably want both: query-based detection and vendor monitoring.

[14:25] Elaine Wu: Can you clarify again retention and deletion semantics? Like if we delete a user, do audit logs delete?
[14:31] Kevin Osei: Audit logs are immutable records for security. We don’t delete historical audit events when an identity is deleted. We may pseudonymize or reference by stable ID. That’s standard for compliance.
[14:44] Elaine Wu: Ok.

[14:47] Priya Shah: What fields are considered “sensitive” and redacted?
[14:51] Kevin Osei: Anything like raw tokens, passwords, private keys, prompt content, model outputs, request bodies — prohibited. For IP/user agent, we include where justified; we don’t include precise geo enrichment. For emails, generally avoided.
[15:09] Priya Shah: Good.

[15:12] Tom Alvarez: For Splunk HEC, do you support mTLS?
[15:16] Colin O'Donnell: Not in beta. We do TLS with server cert validation. If mTLS is required, we should capture that as a follow-on requirement.
[15:25] Tom Alvarez: Ok, not a blocker for dev.

[15:29] Mark Denson: Event volume: do you have ballparks? We need to size indexes.
[15:35] Liam O'Rourke: We can provide rough estimates based on your usage. For most teams it’s not massive, but if you do high-volume API activity, it can add up.
[15:44] Colin O'Donnell: Also, the exporter batches — you’ll see bursts rather than one event per HTTP request.
[15:52] Mark Denson: Right.

[15:55] Priya Shah: Do you have an allow/deny filter? We might not want billing events in Splunk.
[16:00] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. Filters support allowlist and denylist by category and action. You can also filter by actor type or resource type. We recommend default: allow security-relevant categories and block noisy ones.
[16:16] Priya Shah: Is filtering evaluated at export time or at ingestion time?
[16:20] Colin O'Donnell: In the exporter. Config is validated in the control plane API; evaluation occurs in exporter on the stream.
[16:29] Priya Shah: Okay.

[16:32] Elaine Wu: For compliance evidence, we need: description of audit log content, retention period, export guarantees, encryption, and RBAC. Can Redwood provide an FAQ doc?
[16:42] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, we have a security FAQ specifically for the beta. We’ll send it, and we can tailor wording for your questionnaire.
[16:50] Kevin Osei: We’ll also include the “beta limitation” statement: at-least-once delivery; 7-day backfill; no private/on-prem in beta.

[17:02] Mark Denson: About dedupe: If I get duplicates, are the timestamps identical?
[17:07] Colin O'Donnell: emitted_at stays the same. In Splunk you might see different _indextime, obviously. But the payload’s timestamps should be stable.
[17:17] Mark Denson: Great.

[17:20] Priya Shah: How do you prevent partial batch loss? Like if you send 500 events and network drops.
[17:27] Colin O'Donnell: We batch, but checkpointing is based on “acknowledged” deliveries. If a batch fails, it will retry. That’s where duplicates can occur if Splunk accepted some events but failed the request. So again: dedupe by event_id.
[17:45] Priya Shah: Makes sense.

[17:48] Tom Alvarez: For outbound, do you support proxy settings? We have an outbound proxy in some environments.
[17:54] Colin O'Donnell: In hosted, we don’t support customer-specific proxies for exporter egress in beta. In dedicated, we have more flexibility. But for now, easiest is: expose HEC endpoint to our egress IPs.
[18:10] Tom Alvarez: Okay.

[18:12] Elaine Wu: Are audit export config changes logged as well? You said yes, but do you log “test connection” actions?
[18:19] Kevin Osei: Yes, test connection triggers an audit event too, indicating it was executed and whether it succeeded, without exposing secrets.
[18:28] Elaine Wu: Great.

[18:31] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we can walk through a concrete flow. Colin, how does Acme set it up?
[18:37] Colin O'Donnell: In Console, under Settings → Audit Exports (beta), an Org Admin creates a destination: Splunk HEC URL, token reference, optional index/source/sourcetype, and filters. Then you run Test Connection, then enable. Status page shows lag and last error.
[18:57] Priya Shah: Token reference — meaning we paste the token in console?
[19:02] Colin O'Donnell: In beta, yes, you paste it in a secure field and it gets stored encrypted. Longer term there’s roadmap for secret manager integrations.
[19:13] Priya Shah: Ok.

[19:15] Mark Denson: Can you send to multiple destinations? Like Splunk + S3 archive.
[19:20] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, multiple exports per tenant are supported. Each has its own filters and checkpoints.
[19:27] Elaine Wu: But RBAC needs to control that. We don’t want proliferation.
[19:31] Kevin Osei: Right, it’s governed by “manage audit exports” permission.

[19:37] Priya Shah: On PII: user agent can contain weird things. Do you sanitize?
[19:43] Kevin Osei: We store it as-is when present, but we cap length and we do not include request headers beyond user agent. If your policy requires not collecting it, we should discuss — today it’s not a tenant-level toggle, but we can mark as a requirement.
[20:02] Priya Shah: Understood.

[20:05] Tom Alvarez: Any support for customer-managed keys, like bring-your-own KMS?
[20:10] Kevin Osei: For hosted, secrets are stored under Redwood-managed KMS keys. For dedicated/private we can discuss customer-managed keys; again, not in scope for beta, but it’s on the enterprise roadmap.
[20:25] Elaine Wu: Okay.

[20:27] Mark Denson: I want to confirm what fields we can use in Splunk for correlation. actor.id, action, resource.id, outcome, source_ip sometimes, and event_id. Correct?
[20:37] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. And category helps a lot for use cases.
[20:41] Mark Denson: Perfect.

[20:44] Priya Shah: Can you give examples of events? Like API key created, role changed, export paused.
[20:50] Kevin Osei: Yep. We’ll send sample JSON events. For example: “rbac.role.updated”, “api_key.created”, “audit_export.destination.updated”, “audit_export.delivery.paused”.
[21:06] Priya Shah: Great.

[21:09] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else on compliance / evidence?
[21:12] Elaine Wu: We’ll need a statement about SOC2 mapping: like this supports logging/monitoring controls, but it’s not a substitute for our own monitoring. Also what you said about customer responsibility for downstream retention.
[21:26] Kevin Osei: Yes, we can provide that phrasing.

[21:30] Priya Shah: One more: Can you guarantee “no loss” within retention? Or do you hedge.
[21:36] Colin O'Donnell: For beta, we don’t offer contractual guarantee. We do engineering target: deliver with at-least-once semantics, retries, and checkpointing. We track exporter lag and delivery success rate internally. For GA, we expect to attach SLOs.
[21:54] Priya Shah: Ok, that’s an important nuance.

[21:57] Mark Denson: If the exporter pauses, do we get notified?
[22:01] Liam O'Rourke: During beta, we’ll monitor and notify via support channel / email. Not automatic webhook yet.
[22:08] Mark Denson: Fine.

[22:10] Tom Alvarez: Splunk HEC endpoints: ours are behind a load balancer, TLS cert from our internal CA. Will that work?
[22:18] Colin O'Donnell: If it’s an internal CA not publicly trusted, our exporter likely won’t trust it. We need publicly trusted cert chain, or we need to discuss dedicated with custom trust store. For hosted beta, it’s public trust only.
[22:34] Tom Alvarez: Good catch. Our dev HEC does have a public cert. Prod might be internal.
[22:40] Priya Shah: We can start with dev.

[22:43] Liam O'Rourke: Great — thanks for flagging early.

[22:47] Elaine Wu: How about support access: can Redwood view our audit events?
[22:52] Kevin Osei: Support can access limited operational logs and metrics. Access to raw audit event payloads is restricted and audited. For troubleshooting, we generally ask customers to provide sample event_id and timestamps rather than us browsing payloads.
[23:08] Priya Shah: Ok.

[23:10] Mark Denson: Are there any known gaps? Like event coverage.
[23:14] Kevin Osei: Coverage is good for admin/security actions: auth, RBAC, key changes, export changes, model deployment config changes. There are always gaps — we’re expanding categories. We also have a process for adding new event types with security review.
[23:30] Mark Denson: Alright.

[23:32] Liam O'Rourke: I think we’ve hit the big topics. I want to do a quick recap and then action items.
[23:38] Liam O'Rourke: Recap: audit schema v2 with stable event_id, categories, actor/action/resource. Export to Splunk HEC is push, TLS-only, at-least-once with retries, duplicates possible, dedupe by event_id. Beta has 7-day backfill window; Redwood retains audit logs 90 days; customer retains in Splunk. RBAC: manage vs view permissions; config changes are audited. Encryption: tokens stored encrypted via KMS-backed secrets store; redaction in logs.
[24:10] Priya Shah: That matches my notes.

[24:13] Liam O'Rourke: Action items: Redwood will send the beta Security FAQ and evidence language, sample events, and Splunk setup guidance. Acme will confirm Splunk endpoint details, egress allowlist needs, and conventions for index/sourcetype.
[24:28] Tom Alvarez: And we’ll confirm the cert situation for prod.
[24:32] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, thank you.

[24:35] Elaine Wu: Can you also include the limitation statement explicitly: no mTLS, no private support.
[24:41] Liam O'Rourke: Yep.

[24:44] Mark Denson: And if you can, include a suggested Splunk search to verify ingestion.
[24:49] Colin O'Donnell: Will do.

[24:52] Liam O'Rourke: Great. We’ll follow up via email. Thanks everyone.
[24:57] Priya Shah: Thanks.
[24:58] Mark Denson: Thank you.
[25:00] Elaine Wu: Thanks.
[25:01] Tom Alvarez: Bye.

(Recording ended early; remaining scheduled time unused.)
